transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?
I can’t slow down—I have too many important things to take care of and I feel driven to keep doing more, day and night. It feels like if I stop for even a second, everything will just fall apart.
How long have you been feeling this way? Has this high energy and need to keep moving been going on for days, weeks, or longer?

This intense, overcharged feeling has been going on for about two months now. It really started building up when I took on extra shifts at the facility and began coordinating all of my parents' medical appointments.
Have you ever had a period of feeling unusually irritable, high, or euphoric for several days or longer, along with needing less sleep but still having lots of energy?

Yes, for about two months now, I've felt completely cranked up, like I'm running on electricity without needing to sleep. Sometimes I'm overly cheerful and telling everyone how amazing I am at keeping things safe, but then I'll suddenly snap at my husband or coworkers if they get in my way. It has been a constant, intense state during this whole time.
Have you had any previous episodes of feeling this way, or times when your mood was very low or depressed for a period of time?

I don't recall ever having periods of very low mood, and I've never felt this incredibly revved up in the past either. Before this all started a couple of months ago, I mostly just felt like my normal, calmer self.
Have you ever had a period of feeling so down, hopeless, or uninterested in things for two weeks or more that it affected your daily life?

No, I've never really experienced periods of feeling down, hopeless, or uninterested like that. Right now, I'm just completely focused on this high-energy state and having so much that I need to get done.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a current episode of hypomania lasting at least two months, characterized by elevated mood, increased energy, decreased need for sleep, irritability, and goal-directed activity, without a history of prior hypomanic or depressive episodes. The episode is not better explained by an adjustment disorder or brief psychotic episode, and there is no functional impairment severe enough to indicate mania with psychotic features or hospitalization. The onset is linked to psychosocial stressors but exceeds typical stress response in duration and symptom profile, supporting bipolar II disorder, current hypomanic episode.
